stage_a_grounded_agreement_rate.numerator: nodes where all 3 models returned grounded==true AND the LLM judge found semantic agreement
stage_a_grounded_agreement_rate.denominator: all demo-corpus nodes attempted this run
stage_a_grounded_agreement_rate.basis: does NOT require citation verification or a clean adversarial check -- purely: did the 3 models derive the same rule from the cited text, independently.

citation_verification_rate.numerator: nodes where every cited source with a url verified as a substring of the fetched page (round 35: a citation intentionally built with url=None -- general legal-doctrine/judicial-gloss references with no single pinpoint source -- does not count against this; only a genuine mismatch on a citation that DOES have a url blocks this node)
citation_verification_rate.denominator: all demo-corpus nodes attempted this run (null/not computed if --skip-citation-check)
citation_verification_rate.basis: mechanical HTTP fetch + substring match, no model involved.

stage_b_parse_success_rate.numerator: nodes where the adversarial call returned parseable edge_cases (not truncated, not empty, no error) -- even after the round-23/24 retry
stage_b_parse_success_rate.denominator: all demo-corpus nodes attempted this run
stage_b_parse_success_rate.basis: an infrastructure/reliability signal, not a gap-count -- a node can parse successfully and still expose real gaps, or fail to parse and expose none we know of.

full_pipeline_clean_pass_rate.stage: all three stages combined -- this is the renamed former 'grounded_agreement_rate' (round 26; the old name was found to be mislabeled relative to its own definition, see docs/DEBT_PROJECT_ARCHITECTURE_SPEC.md S4's round-24 entry)
full_pipeline_clean_pass_rate.denominator: all demo-corpus nodes attempted this run
full_pipeline_clean_pass_rate.basis: CLEAN-PASS = LLM-judged semantic agreement across all 3 grounded derivations AND all citations live-verified AND no adversarial gap found AND the adversarial check itself parsed successfully (round 26 -- a Stage B parse failure no longer silently reads as "no gaps", see spec S4). Numeric fingerprint is a secondary diagnostic only as of 2026-08-26 round 3, not part of this basis either.

grounded_agreement_rate.note: Deprecated alias for full_pipeline_clean_pass_rate (round 26), kept only so anything still reading this exact key doesn't break. This name was found to be mislabeled -- it was never actually a Stage-A-only measure despite the name. Use full_pipeline_clean_pass_rate (the honest name for the same number) or stage_a_grounded_agreement_rate (genuinely Stage-A-only) going forward.

scenario_pass_rate.stage: scenario level (depends on multiple nodes' CLEAN-PASS status)
scenario_pass_rate.numerator: concept-demo scenarios where every node_id they depend on is CLEAN-PASS this run
scenario_pass_rate.denominator: all concept-demo scenarios defined in the scenarios file
scenario_pass_rate.basis: a scenario passes iff every node_id it depends on is CLEAN-PASS in this same run

undispositioned_material_findings.stage: Stage B, net of the disposition ledger

results.derivation_summary: Under 12 C.F.R. § 1006.14(b)(2)(i), a debt collector is presumed to comply with the harassment prohibition (and FDCPA § 806(5)) if it places calls to a particular person about a particular debt neither more than seven times in seven consecutive days nor within seven consecutive days after having had a telephone conversation with that person about that debt (the conversation date counts as day one). Conversely, under (b)(2)(ii), exceeding either frequency creates a presumption of violation. The counts are per person and per 'particular debt' (each debt in collection, except student loans serviced under one account number, which count as one debt under (b)(4)), and calls excluded by (b)(3) — those placed with prior consent within seven days, calls not connected to the dialed number, and calls to persons in § 1006.6(d)(1)(ii)–(vi) — do not count. Note that a stricter state rule, 940 CMR 7.04(1)(f), limits telephone communications to two per seven-day period at the debtor's personal numbers for each debt.

diagnostics.text_at_break_point: nitiating a communication with any debto

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer has five separate medical accounts placed with the same collection agency. The agency calls her cell phone about each account 5-6 times per week, totaling roughly 28 calls in a single 7-day period, but never more than 6 per individual account.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node counts strictly per-debt and would output 'presumptively compliant' for a person receiving ~28 calls a week from one collector. Multiple accounts placed with a single agency (medical, telecom, retail card portfolios) is extremely common. The node's only hedge is a passing line that a consumer might rebut the presumption 'in an unusual case' -- but high-volume multi-debt calling is not unusual, and there is no cross-reference to the 15 U.S.C. 1692d(5) harassment standard, no checklist item asking for total call volume across all debts with the same collector, and no instruction to evaluate the aggregate pattern. A consumer with a strong 1692d(5) claim would be told her situation is presumptively lawful.

edge_cases.scenario: The consumer herself phones the collector on Monday to dispute the balance and speaks with a representative for ten minutes. The collector then places three calls to her on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. She never asked to be called back.
edge_cases.gap_description: The post-conversation 7-day cooldown is triggered by 'having had a telephone conversation' regardless of who placed the call, so all three follow-up calls are presumptive violations. But the checklist's fact-gathering is framed entirely around outbound contacts: item 1 asks for 'calls FROM this collector' and item 2 asks whether 'any of THOSE contacts' were conversations. A consumer-initiated conversation therefore never enters the fact set, the cooldown is never detected, and the node outputs 'presumptively compliant' (only 3 calls) on a fact pattern that is a clear presumptive violation. Consumers calling in to dispute, negotiate, or set up payment is one of the most common ways a conversation occurs.

edge_cases.scenario: A collector cannot reach the consumer, so it calls her husband's cell phone four times in one week and tells him the balance owed on her credit card. The consumer asks whether the calls to her husband were unlawful.
edge_cases.gap_description: The third_party_communication_note states flatly that 'a pattern of repeated calls to a relative that mention the debt' is 'very likely a separate, more direct FDCPA violation under 1692c(b)/1692b.' That is wrong for a spouse: 15 U.S.C. 1692c(d) defines 'consumer' for purposes of 1692c to include the consumer's spouse (and the parent of a minor, guardian, executor, or administrator), so communications with a spouse are not third-party communications under 1692c(b) at all -- they are instead governed by the ordinary consumer-contact rules. The node has no 1692c(d) carve-out and no checklist item distinguishing a spouse/guardian/executor from an ordinary third party, so it would tell a consumer (or a collector) that plainly permitted spousal contact is very likely unlawful, and would conversely mis-analyze whether those calls should be assessed under the consumer-facing 1692c(a)/(c) rules. Collectors reaching spouses on joint or household accounts is very common.

results.derivation_summary: Under §1692a(6), a person is a "debt collector" only if the principal purpose of its business is collecting debts, or if it regularly collects debts "owed or due another" — so, as Henson holds, a company collecting debts it purchased for its own account is not covered on that second prong (the Court left the "principal purpose" prong open). The obligation must also be a "debt" under §1692a(5): a consumer's obligation to pay money arising from a transaction primarily for personal, family, or household purposes, owed by a natural person consumer (§1692a(3)). A "creditor" under §1692a(4) is one who extends credit or is owed the debt, excluding a person who takes assignment of a debt already in default solely to facilitate collection for another; creditors collecting their own debts are outside coverage unless they use a false third-party name, and §1692a(6)(A)–(F) exempts, among others, employees of the creditor, affiliated collectors, government officers, process servers, nonprofit credit counselors, and those handling debts not in default when obtained or originated by them. Per Obduskey, a business doing no more than nonjudicial foreclosure/security-interest enforcement is a debt collector only for purposes of §1692f(6).
results.citation_used: 15 U.S.C. § 1692a(3)-(6); Henson v. Santander Consumer USA Inc., 582 U.S. ___ (2017); Obduskey v. McCarthy & Holthus LLP, 587 U.S. ___ (2019)

results.derivation_summary: Under the FDCPA, a "debt collector" is a person whose principal business is collecting debts, or who regularly collects debts owed to another. The term generally does not include the original creditor collecting their own debt, or a company that purchased a debt and is collecting it for itself. The act applies to "debts" which are consumer obligations arising from transactions for personal, family, or household purposes.

semantic_agreement_judge.agreement_notes: All three give the same core definitions: 'debt collector' = principal-purpose collector or one who regularly collects debts owed another; 'debt' = consumer obligation from a personal/family/household transaction; and all agree Henson means a purchaser collecting for its own account isn't covered under the 'owed another' prong, with Obduskey limiting pure nonjudicial foreclosure activity to § 1692f(6) (Analysis 3 omits Obduskey). Completeness note: Analysis 3 states flatly that debt buyers are excluded, whereas Analyses 1 and 2 more precisely note the 'principal purpose' prong was left open by Henson and list the § 1692a(6)(A)-(F) exclusions and the § 1692a(4) creditor/assignee carve-out — an omission/oversimplification rather than a contradiction.

results.derivation_summary: Under Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 337(a), an action on any contract, obligation, or liability founded on a written instrument must be brought within four years (with a special three-month limit for deficiency-type money judgments after a trustee's/mortgage power-of-sale sale, and an exception under § 336a). Once that four-year period has run, § 337(d) bars anyone from filing suit or initiating arbitration or other proceedings to collect the debt, and the period may be extended only under § 360 — i.e., by a signed written acknowledgment or promise, or by a payment of principal or interest, though no payment can revive a claim already barred. Other provisions may adjust the running of the period in particular situations: emergency rule 9(a) tolled limitations periods over 180 days from April 6 to October 1, 2020; 11 U.S.C. § 108(c) extends the period where a bankruptcy stay applies; 50 U.S.C. § 3936(a) excludes a servicemember's period of military service; and § 361 bars suit here if the claim arose in another state and is time-barred there.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer's father died in March 2024 owing $9,000 on a Chase card that went into default in 2022; a debt buyer sends the family a demand in late 2025 and the daughter (who is handling the estate) asks whether the debt is still collectible. The node computes 2022 accrual + 4 years and reports 'not expired.'
edge_cases.gap_description: The node has no screening question for the death of the debtor. CCP § 366.2 imposes a one-year-from-death outer limit on any cause of action on a decedent's personal liability 'whether accrued or not accrued,' and it applies notwithstanding any longer statute and is not tolled by the ordinary tolling provisions. Deceased-relative debt inquiries are among the most common consumer-debt questions actually presented. Here the node's 'not expired' output is flatly wrong (the claim died in March 2025) and pushes a family toward paying a barred debt; the same omission also runs the other direction, since a creditor with a fresh default has only one year, not four, once the debtor dies.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer discovers a default judgment entered against her in 2013 on a Cap One card when a collector serves a new wage garnishment in 2026; the judgment was never renewed. She asks whether the collector can still collect. The node routes her to judgment_enforcement_note, which tells her the judgment is enforceable for 10 years from entry and 'renewable for additional 10-year periods without limit.'
edge_cases.gap_description: The judgment_enforcement_note captures the 10-year period and unlimited renewability but omits the dispositive corollary: under CCP §§ 683.020 and 683.130, the renewal application must be filed BEFORE the 10 years expire; an un-renewed judgment becomes unenforceable and cannot be revived. There is no checklist item asking whether the judgment was renewed or when it was entered relative to today. Old, never-renewed default judgments that resurface via garnishment or credit-report review are extremely common in California consumer-debt practice, and the node as written tells a consumer with a dead 2013 judgment that it is live and perpetually renewable — the opposite of the correct answer, and in the direction that costs her money.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer defaulted on a written retail-installment contract on July 15, 2020 (accrual squarely inside the Emergency Rule 9 tolling window). The collector files suit November 20, 2024. The node applies its flat conditional +178 days (accrual before October 1, 2020 and deadline not passed before April 6, 2020) and reports the suit timely to roughly January 9, 2025.
edge_cases.gap_description: The determination grants a flat 178 days to every claim accruing before October 1, 2020, but tolling only suspends a clock that is actually running. A claim accruing mid-window (April 6 – September 30, 2020) never had its clock running for the earlier part of the window, so it gains only the days from accrual to October 1, 2020 — here about 78 days, giving a real deadline near October 1, 2024, not January 2025. The node therefore tells a consumer with a genuinely expired claim that the November 2024 suit is timely, i.e., that she has no limitations defense when she does. The window is a six-month band of peak-COVID defaults now hitting their four-year mark in 2024–25 filings, so boundary cases are not rare, and the error can be up to nearly six months.
